requirements.statement: Capture sponsor, business owner, subject-matter experts, security, data, operations, and end-user roles.
Model happy paths, exception paths, handoffs, approvals, and undocumented workarounds.
Separate observed facts, stakeholder claims, assumptions, conflicts, and unknowns.
Link every proposed opportunity to a baseline metric and accountable owner.
Persist decisions and action items with due dates and evidence references.
Measure current cycle time, labor, defects, incidents, revenue leakage, and risk exposure where relevant.
Use ranges and confidence levels when data is incomplete.
Keep model, compute, storage, network, and human-review costs separate.
Express delivery estimates as machine wall-clock plus explicitly separate human decisions.
Define post-launch measurement ownership, cadence, and data source.
Classify engagement phase as discovery, PoC, pilot, production, remediation, or handoff.
Define in-scope, out-of-scope, dependencies, customer responsibilities, and non-goals.
Make acceptance criteria machine-verifiable where possible.
Define stop, escalation, rollback, and re-scope conditions.
Bind scope to exact repositories, environments, data classes, and authority boundaries.
Derive status from execution and evidence ledgers rather than agent self-report.
Report scope, progress, risks, blockers, decisions, cost, machine wall-clock, and next gates.
Distinguish completed, in-progress, blocked, unknown, unsupported, and waived work.
Escalate material changes to security, correctness, schedule, or acceptance confidence.
Keep executive and engineering views consistent through shared identifiers.
Answer only from versioned product, deployment, policy, and evidence sources.
Mark unsupported, planned, customer-responsibility, and release-time-configured controls distinctly.
Route legal and regulatory interpretations to authorized humans.
Prevent reuse of stale answers after architecture or policy changes.
Produce a gap and remediation plan for unanswered requirements.
Segment users by role, workflow, risk, and readiness.
Define enablement, pilot cohorts, champions, office hours, and support channels.
Measure activation, repeat use, completion, intervention, and business outcomes.
Capture feedback with consent and tenant-specific data-use controls.
Create an operational ownership and knowledge-transfer exit plan.
Verify tenant, repository, branch, commit, submodule, LFS, and artifact authorization before access.
Create an immutable RevisionSet covering every repository and external artifact used by the task.
Preserve source integrity and separate read-only intake from writable transformation workspaces.
Hash imported files, manifests, archives, and generated inventories.
Block analysis when repository identity or custody is ambiguous.
Classify every file and directory with confidence, origin, ownership, and processing policy.
Detect languages, frameworks, build systems, package managers, schemas, IaC, CI/CD, and test assets.
Identify generated, vendored, duplicated, encrypted, binary, ignored, and unreachable assets.
Map monorepo, polyrepo, service, module, package, and deployable-unit boundaries.
Report unclassified and inaccessible assets as explicit unknowns.
Resolve language runtimes, compilers, SDKs, system packages, build tools, private registries, and environment variables.
Pin exact versions and immutable images or digests before evidence is reusable.
Distinguish source defects from environment, network, credential, and dependency failures.
Capture commands, logs, artifacts, resource limits, and environment hashes for replay.
Use environment-owned authority and reject inherited thread-global privileges.
Inventory every external dependency, protocol, authentication method, side effect, and availability assumption.
Choose record-replay, contract stub, emulator, container, simulator, or real test service by risk and fidelity.
Declare unsupported behavior and fidelity gaps.
Prevent test doubles from being mistaken for production evidence.
Redact sensitive captured traffic and bind fixtures to consent and retention rules.
Score every relevant language, framework, database, protocol, and runtime from S0 to S5.
Track analysis coverage by file, module, behavior, environment, issue domain, and evidence source.
Register UNKNOWN, UNSUPPORTED, inaccessible, ambiguous, and stale-evidence states separately.
Block completion claims when critical unknowns or unsupported paths affect acceptance criteria.
Publish an honest completeness statement with assumptions and blind spots.
Require explicit environment, data, user, duration, and purpose authorization before capture.
Correlate telemetry to exact build, configuration, RevisionSet, request, user role, and workflow.
Redact secrets and regulated data before model-visible processing.
Preserve sampling, loss, clock, and instrumentation limitations.
Generate replayable, normalized behavioral evidence without duplicating production side effects.
Parse supported assets into lossless syntax and typed semantic representations while preserving source locations.
Resolve symbols, types, calls, control flow, data flow, exceptions, concurrency, transactions, events, and side effects.
Link code to build, runtime, database, API, infrastructure, tests, and generated artifacts.
Represent ambiguous dynamic dispatch, reflection, macros, code generation, and native boundaries as candidate edges with confidence.
Support incremental rebuilds keyed by RevisionSet and analyzer versions.
Link each approved workflow step to implementing modules, endpoints, queries, events, screens, and tests.
Extract explicit and implicit rules, decision tables, state transitions, calculations, and exception policies.
Record conflicting implementations and undocumented behavior.
Associate business criticality, users, data classes, and owners with technical components.
Maintain traceability across revisions and transformations.
Track sources, transformations, stores, caches, exports, logs, models, and deletion paths for sensitive and critical data.
Trace events from producer through broker, retries, consumers, databases, and external effects.
Trace identity, role, policy, tenant, delegation, and service-account context through each hop.
Detect context loss, cross-tenant paths, authorization gaps, and untracked side effects.
Bind lineage edges to static and runtime evidence with confidence and retention classification.
Analyze co-change, churn, defect linkage, reverts, release branches, and migration sequences.
Distinguish generated mass changes from meaningful coupling.
Identify ownership concentration and orphaned critical modules without employee scoring.
Link historical incidents and decisions to current code when evidence exists.
Respect privacy, labor, and retention policies for contributor data.
Represent source, method, version, scope, freshness, confidence, and limitations for every fact.
Prefer authoritative deterministic evidence for questions it can decide.
Retain contradictions and counterexamples instead of collapsing them prematurely.
Invalidate facts when RevisionSet, environment, toolchain, policy, or analyzer versions change.
Generate proof obligations for facts that remain material but uncertain.
Use one ontology across business correctness, code, architecture, data, security, reliability, tests, infrastructure, AI, UX, and operations.
Require location, evidence, trigger condition, impact, likelihood, confidence, root cause, remediation, and verification plan.
Deduplicate, correlate, and cluster symptoms under evidence-supported root causes.
Preserve source-tool identifiers, suppressed results, waivers, and false-positive rationale.
Link findings to business capabilities, invariants, acceptance criteria, and affected revisions.
Detect cyclic dependencies, layer violations, unstable boundaries, shared data coupling, distributed monoliths, and change hotspots.
Assess cohesion, coupling, complexity, duplication, dead code, wrong abstraction, and framework leakage.
Compare implemented structure with documented architecture and repository rules.
Prioritize debt by change frequency, criticality, defect history, and transformation leverage.
Propose executable architecture fitness functions for consequential rules.
Analyze nullability, bounds, numeric precision, time, locale, error, resource, and lifecycle behavior.
Detect races, deadlocks, atomicity violations, lost updates, unsafe publication, and cancellation leaks.
Trace transaction, retry, timeout, idempotency, ordering, deduplication, compensation, and cache consistency.
Recover and validate business state machines and conservation invariants.
Use tests, replay, fuzzing, symbolic reasoning, or formal methods according to risk.
Model assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, data classes, abuse cases, and side effects.
Trace authentication, authorization, service identity, tenant context, and privileged paths end to end.
Detect common application, API, agent, dependency, artifact, CI/CD, container, cloud, and IaC risks.
Generate SBOM, dependency delta, license delta, and provenance obligations where tooling exists.
Separate product controls, deployment controls, organizational controls, and customer responsibilities.
Recover logical and physical schemas, constraints, indexes, routines, triggers, views, permissions, and ownership.
Analyze query plans, N+1 patterns, transaction boundaries, locking, pagination, and data-access anti-patterns.
Detect data-quality, retention, deletion, PII, lineage, and reconciliation gaps.
Assess expand-migrate-contract, CDC, backfill, dual-write, rollback, and cutover hazards.
Compare dialect and routine semantics rather than syntax alone.
Assess algorithmic complexity, CPU, memory, GC, I/O, locks, connections, queues, caches, batching, and backpressure.
Evaluate timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, failover, backup, restore, disaster recovery, and graceful degradation.
Map service-level indicators, objectives, error budgets, dashboards, alerts, traces, logs, metrics, and profiles.
Use representative workload models and preserve hardware, dataset, configuration, and sampling identity.
Estimate cost and capacity impact of remediation options.
Map business-critical behaviors to unit, integration, contract, end-to-end, property, mutation, performance, and security tests.
Detect weak assertions, overmocking, shared-state pollution, non-determinism, flaky timing, and unrealistic fixtures.
Assess build graph efficiency, caching, parallelism, hermeticity, artifact promotion, branch protection, and rollback readiness.
Track developer feedback latency and repeated failure causes.
Recommend hard enforcement for deterministic rules and review guidance for judgment-based rules.
Trace critical user journeys across routes, states, forms, errors, permissions, network failures, and recovery.
Assess keyboard, screen-reader, contrast, semantics, focus, motion, and accessible error handling using automated and manual evidence.
Detect hard-coded locale, timezone, currency, encoding, pluralization, and bidirectional-text assumptions.
Measure bundle, rendering, data-fetch, hydration, memory, and interaction performance.
Link experience findings to adoption and business outcomes.
Inventory models, prompts, policies, retrieval, memory, tools, agents, workflows, datasets, and evaluators with versions.
Test task success, grounding, citation, tool choice, recovery, latency, cost, and human intervention.
Assess prompt injection, indirect injection, tool escalation, data exfiltration, memory poisoning, and tenant leakage.
Detect evaluator leakage, weak or circular judges, missing holdouts, and non-reproducible model changes.
Require independent evidence and explicit model/provider/version pins for reusable results.
Attribute cost to tenant, engagement, repository, workflow, step, model, tool, environment, and artifact.
Separate model, compute, storage, network, license, and human-review costs.
Detect retry waste, duplicate analysis, poor cache reuse, idle workers, oversized resources, and expensive low-value evidence.
Model cost-quality-latency-risk tradeoffs without violating acceptance or safety gates.
Track machine wall-clock and queue time separately from human elapsed time.
Separate symptoms, contributing conditions, root causes, amplifiers, and latent risks.
Prioritize using business criticality, likelihood, blast radius, exploitability, change frequency, and remediation leverage.
Account for prerequisite fixes, coupled findings, and risk introduced by change.
Keep evidence confidence and unknowns visible in ranking.
Produce quick wins, mandatory controls, enabling foundations, and strategic workstreams.
Derive candidate invariants from requirements, code, tests, data, traces, incidents, policies, and domain experts.
Distinguish required behavior, accidental behavior, known defect, tolerated deviation, and desired change.
Express invariants as executable contracts, test oracles, temporal properties, schemas, or formal properties where possible.
Attach scope, assumptions, owner, evidence, confidence, and change-approval rules.
Block transformation of critical behavior without an approved invariant or explicit risk acceptance.
Generate at least conservative, balanced, and strategic alternatives when material architecture change is proposed.
Define module and service boundaries, data ownership, APIs, events, identity, deployment, observability, and operational ownership.
Map every design decision to root causes, invariants, acceptance criteria, and constraints.
Quantify reversibility, migration risk, machine wall-clock, cost, and organizational impact.
Document assumptions, rejected alternatives, review date, and exit triggers in ADRs.
Represent every step with preconditions, scope, expected changes, tools, authority, checkpoint, tests, evidence, side effects, and rollback.
Order contract, characterization, data, compatibility, and observability work before risky replacement steps.
Identify safe parallel read work and isolate write work through worktrees or non-overlapping scopes.
Calculate critical-path machine wall-clock separately from queue and human-review time.
Re-plan when evidence, revisions, failures, or approvals change.
Each ChangeSet must have one purpose, bounded files, linked findings, invariants, plan step, tests, evidence, and rollback.
Record agent, model, tool, prompt or recipe, environment, input and output hashes, and approvals.
Intercept tool results before commit and reject unexpected file or side-effect deltas.
Prevent self-approval by the producing agent and preserve independent review.
Support staged integration, conflict detection, revert, and compensation without rewriting audit history.
Prefer compiler refactoring APIs, typed LST or AST recipes, and Semantic IR transformations over free-form patches.
Bind each execution to an invocation-scoped capability lease and environment-owned authority.
Checkpoint before side effects and after each accepted atomic ChangeSet.
Generate or update tests and observability before changing high-risk behavior.
Stop, compensate, or roll back when proof obligations fail or scope drifts.
Classify work as repair, refactor, modernization, rearchitecture, or rewrite and apply the matching proof burden.
Preserve external contracts through adapters, façades, dual routes, feature flags, or compatibility layers.
Migrate by business capability and observable traffic rather than arbitrary file groups.
Plan data ownership, backfill, dual-write, event, and rollback semantics before cutover.
Retire legacy components only after usage, equivalence, and recovery evidence satisfy policy.
Extract source behavior, type, concurrency, error, resource, serialization, build, and framework semantics into versioned IR.
Map constructs through route-specific semantic rules and explicitly register non-isomorphic gaps.
Generate idiomatic target architecture and code without weakening required behavior.
Compile and run source and target in native toolchains with normalized traces.
Require route-specific fixtures, holdouts, and rollback before replacing source systems.
Model source and target types, nulls, collation, precision, transaction, locking, routine, trigger, sequence, and error semantics.
Generate expand-migrate-contract steps, backfills, CDC, compatibility views, dual reads or writes, and rollback.
Reconcile row counts, keys, relationships, states, monetary totals, checksums, and domain invariants.
Preserve or explicitly re-approve authorization, ownership, audit, retention, and deletion behavior.
Validate application queries, ORMs, reports, and operational procedures against the target engine.
Derive verification obligations from acceptance criteria, invariants, findings, changes, and risk.
Compare source and target values, errors, data mutations, events, side effects, states, timing, and user-visible behavior under normalized semantics.
Classify differences as exact failure, normalized equivalence, tolerated range, approved change, unknown, or oracle defect.
Evaluate test strength through mutation or equivalent fault seeding on critical paths.
Keep verifier execution and completion decisions independent from the producer.
Select formal methods only where risk, tractability, and property shape justify them.
Represent modeling assumptions, abstractions, environment constraints, and trusted components explicitly.
Check state safety, liveness, concurrency, permissions, conservation, migration mapping, or protocol behavior as applicable.
Store proof artifacts, checker versions, commands, results, counterexamples, and translation links.
Use proof results as evidence inputs, never as blanket system certification.

E0 requires asset and RevisionSet identity; E1 requires reproducible native build status; E2 requires approved behavior and test evidence; E3 requires non-functional, security, migration, and recovery readiness evidence.
Bind every claim to exact repository, environment, model, tool, database, policy, and artifact versions.
Block UNKNOWN, UNSUPPORTED, stale evidence, unresolved critical side effects, and missing approvals.
Ensure K8 or equivalent independent completion authority makes the decision.
State clearly that this capability package cannot issue E4, E5, P05, customer, regulatory, or accredited certification.
Define cohorts, traffic percentages, observation windows, success metrics, error budgets, and automatic rollback triggers.
Prevent shadow or dual runs from duplicating external side effects unless an approved idempotent isolation method exists.
Reconcile behavior, data, events, latency, cost, and user outcomes between old and new paths.
Test rollback, compensation, feature-flag failure, and data compatibility before authorized production use.
Produce a handoff packet for independent E4/E5 execution rather than self-certifying.
Prioritize safety, containment, service restoration, data integrity, and communication before structural improvement.
Use verified security context, incident-specific authority, and explicit command or write approvals.
Build a time-ordered evidence timeline across users, releases, telemetry, dependencies, and side effects.
Separate trigger, root cause, contributing conditions, detection gaps, and recovery gaps.
Convert material lessons into repository rules, skills, scripts, tests, policies, or no change according to ownership.
Package architecture, operation, recovery, security, data, deployment, verification, and known-risk knowledge.
Assign named owners, escalation paths, SLO responsibilities, access, and support windows.
Provide role-specific training and exercises, including failure and rollback scenarios.
Verify runbooks through walkthrough or game-day evidence rather than document existence alone.
Preserve customer-specific confidentiality and data-use restrictions.
Require evidence of recurrence, bounded responsibility, independent validation, and clear ownership before creating a new Skill.
Prefer updating existing instructions, references, scripts, adapters, tests, or policies over adding overlapping capabilities.
Separate tenant-local learning from globally eligible artifacts under explicit consent.
Sanitize examples, remove secrets and identifiers, and preserve provenance and license constraints.
Evaluate trigger precision, workflow correctness, approval boundaries, and regression behavior before release.
Build a portfolio graph of repositories, shared libraries, APIs, data, events, teams, environments, and release dependencies.
Normalize risk and readiness by size, criticality, support depth, evidence coverage, and unknowns.
Identify common root causes, reusable migration waves, shared blockers, and systemic dependencies.
Plan capacity, machine wall-clock, cost, change windows, and rollback domains across programs.
Prevent portfolio rollups from masking repository-specific unsupported or critical conditions.
Normalize requests by user, workflow, problem, business impact, frequency, strategic fit, implementation leverage, and evidence quality.
Separate one-off custom work from reusable product opportunity.
Link requests to findings, adoption data, incidents, lost deals, and existing capabilities.
Preserve tenant confidentiality and aggregate only under permitted policies.
Return decisions and workarounds to delivery teams without implying commitment.
No data, artifact, cache, telemetry, vector, graph, credential, or execution context may cross tenant boundaries.
All tool and connector capabilities are denied unless granted by an invocation-scoped lease.
Authority must belong to the actual execution environment and survive resume without widening.
Privileged requests must carry a host-minted, integrity-protected security context.
Replaced or stale executors must be unable to commit results or effects.
Every tool result must be intercepted, typed, policy-checked, and attached to the correct invocation before commit.
Repository changes must be purpose-bounded, independently verifiable, and individually reversible.
Retry or resume must not duplicate repository, database, message, billing, or external side effects.
Accepted progress must survive process, worker, and network failure according to the task durability class.
Long-running jobs must support bounded cancellation and explicit effect reconciliation.
Every material decision, tool call, artifact, approval, waiver, and state transition must be attributable and queryable.
All source, generated, evidence, model, tool, and deployment artifacts must use immutable content identity.
Evidence reuse must be invalidated by incompatible changes to revisions, environments, policies, tools, models, databases, or adapters.
The producer of a change or claim must not be the sole verifier or completion authority.
Unknown, unsupported, inaccessible, ambiguous, and stale areas must remain visible in all completion statements.
The capability package may claim E3 readiness at most and must never issue E4, E5, P05, regulatory, or customer certification.
Only data necessary for the approved purpose may be read, retained, displayed, or sent to a model.
Secrets must be brokered to tools and never copied into model-visible prompts, logs, or artifacts.
Storage, processing, backup, telemetry, and model routing must honor tenant and engagement residency policy.
Artifacts and derived data must have explicit retention, legal hold, deletion, and cryptographic erasure behavior.
Sensitive data must be encrypted in transit and at rest with customer-appropriate key ownership.
Build inputs, dependencies, images, tools, and outputs require provenance, integrity checks, and policy evaluation.
Schedulers and quotas must prevent one tenant or repository from starving others.
Queues, event streams, model calls, and analysis workers must have bounded concurrency and backpressure.
Interactive control-plane operations should meet the configured p95 latency objective excluding long-running jobs.
Long jobs must emit monotonic, evidence-backed progress and blocker states.
Stateless coordinators and partitionable workers must scale independently without changing semantic ownership.
The architecture must support controlled pilots above 500k LOC and at least one benchmark above 1M LOC before commercial claims.
Unchanged artifacts and compatible evidence should be reused by content identity rather than rescanned blindly.
A run must be reproducible from pinned inputs or explicitly state sources of nondeterminism.
Trace, metrics, structured logs, profiles, policy decisions, and artifact identities must correlate by tenant, engagement, run, step, and revision.
Each production service and workflow requires defined SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, owners, and escalation.
Unavailable models, analyzers, connectors, or services must produce controlled degradation or explicit blockers, never silent omission.
Backup, restore, failover, replay, and disaster-recovery procedures must be testable and evidence-producing.
Public APIs, events, schemas, CLI output, and persisted contracts require versioning and backward-compatibility policy.
Language, framework, database, scanner, model, connector, and runtime integrations must use replaceable adapters.
Adapters may produce candidate artifacts and evidence but cannot own semantic truth or completion status.
User-facing product surfaces must support configured accessibility targets and keyboard-complete critical workflows.
Time, locale, currency, units, encoding, text direction, and translation must be explicit and testable.
Critical FDE and approval workflows must expose evidence, risk, scope, and next action without requiring raw log inspection.
Model, compute, storage, network, license, and human-review costs must be separately attributable.
Estimates and actuals must report machine wall-clock, queue, and human-review time separately.
Tenant, engagement, route, model, tool, and worker budgets require alert, throttle, stop, and approval policies.
Model choice must consider task ambiguity, evidence risk, privacy, latency, cost, and provider policy.
Canonical task, tool, result, evidence, and checkpoint contracts must not depend on one provider.
Noisy or probabilistic evaluations require sample size, variance, uncertainty, segmentation, and decision rules.
Failed cases and contradictory evidence must be retained as first-class artifacts.
Consequential deterministic controls should be enforceable through versioned policy or validation code.
Irreversible, destructive, privileged, regulated, or production-impacting actions require named human approval.
Planning, execution, verification, waiver, and certification roles must be independently assignable.
Each write-heavy agent or plan step must use an isolated workspace or non-overlapping file scope.
Agents should receive a map and task-relevant references rather than a monolithic instruction dump.
Architecture, runbooks, rules, and capability catalogs require owners, freshness checks, and broken-link validation.
Skills require positive, contextual, negative-control, and adjacent-intent eval cases.
Package installation must support dry-run, clean-state checks, backup, receipt, modified-file protection, and reversible uninstall.
Repeated release builds from identical inputs must have stable file sets and hashes.
Schema and contract migrations must be additive-first, replayable, reconciled, and rollback-aware.
The extension must not create a second Goal store, AI-SIR owner, runtime authority, or completion authority.
Billing, quotas, support entitlements, and contract terms must not alter technical evidence or completion results.
Customers must be able to export approved reports, evidence indexes, changes, and runbooks in stable machine-readable formats.
Every capability has one accountable owner and one canonical authority path.
Every Skill is non-routable and is activated only by an existing canonical route owner.
Every Adapter is replaceable and cannot certify its own result.
Every material claim references exact supporting and contradicting evidence.
Every production-impacting effect has an approval, idempotency key, checkpoint, and compensation or rollback strategy.
Every release decision states scope, assumptions, unknowns, unsupported areas, waivers, and invalidation triggers.
Every waiver has a named risk owner, expiry, scope, rationale, compensating control, and revalidation trigger.
Every new Skill passes non-duplication review against the capability graph.
Every reusable learning artifact follows tenant consent, redaction, provenance, and license policy.
Every repository rule includes positive violation, safe counterexample, and unrelated-change tests.
Every Golden Route defines supported versions, fixture corpus, native runtime lab, failure corpus, and readiness gates.
Every machine estimate separates wall-clock, queue, compute cost, model cost, storage, network, and human review.
Every large change is decomposed into reviewable, reversible ChangeSets.
Every critical user journey maps to acceptance criteria, code, data, tests, telemetry, and owner.
Every unknown has impact, owner, resolution path, deadline or accepted permanence, and release effect.
Every external connector declares data classes, read/write authority, side effects, rate limits, and failure semantics.
Every skill, model, tool, policy, adapter, schema, and protocol update triggers scoped evidence invalidation.
Every incident postmortem classifies improvements into AGENTS, harness, Skill, reference, script, test, adapter, policy, new Skill, or no change.
Every E3 result is explicitly distinguished from E4/E5/P05 or customer production certification.
Every customer-facing report derives status from ledgers and evidence rather than plan text or agent self-report.
